name: Laqta clip-selection benchmark v1
description: A small, self-contained benchmark for the deterministic clip ranking. Every item is a narration script split into sentences; each sentence is labelled highlight, context or filler. The media is synthesised from the script (espeak-ng), so the labelled spans are exact and the whole set is reproducible from source — no third-party media is committed.
method: Each sentence is synthesised separately, so its exact time span is known.
The sentences are concatenated into one video with the same narration.
The real pipeline runs on that video: s01_ingest -> s02_transcript -> s04_candidates -> s05_ranking.
A selected clip counts as a hit when it overlaps a labelled highlight span by at least 30% of its own duration (IoU).

precision = hits / selected clips; recall = labelled highlights covered / labelled highlights; coverage = selected seconds / media seconds; bad coverage = selected seconds outside a label / selected seconds.
notes: Every item is at least 90 seconds long, because the shipped configuration only proposes clips between 28 and 58 seconds. A shorter item could never produce a candidate and would measure nothing.
The labelled spans are the sentences, not the clips: a human marking 'this sentence is worth clipping' is a weaker and more reproducible judgement than marking exact clip boundaries.

labels.highlight: A self-contained moment worth clipping on its own.
labels.context: Setup that makes the highlight understandable, but is not worth clipping alone.

items.title: A short talk with two highlights and a long context block

sentences.text: Welcome back to the show, this episode is about keeping a local pipeline fast on a modest laptop.
sentences.label: filler

sentences.text: We are going to talk about how a long recording becomes a handful of clips you can actually post.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: The machine does three things: it listens, it reads, and it cuts, and the order matters more than the speed.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: First, the quick idea that changes everything, the slow model only ever runs on the part you keep.
sentences.label: highlight

sentences.text: So instead of transcribing forty minutes to find one minute, you transcribe one minute to find one minute.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: That is the whole trick, and it is why the tool feels instant on hardware that should not be able to.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: Second, measure the stages instead of guessing, because the stage that feels slow is rarely the stage that is.
sentences.label: highlight

sentences.text: Every stage writes its real wall time into the manifest, so the numbers are measured and not remembered.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: When you look at the report you can see that the model loaded once and then ran for a while, which is fine.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: The mistake people make is tuning the fast stage instead of the slow one, and the report shows that instantly.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: Third, keep the ranking explainable, because a score you cannot argue with is a score you cannot trust.
sentences.label: highlight

sentences.text: Every clip shows the signals that produced it, and the weights add up to exactly one, so nothing is hidden.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: If a signal is missing it does not count as zero, it is redistributed, and the clip says that it was measured less.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: You can disagree with a weight and change it, and the next run will show you what changed.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: That is the difference between a number and an argument, and it is the whole point of the tool.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: Thanks for listening, and we will see you in the next episode.
sentences.label: filler

items.title: A talk about captions and Arabic text, with one clear highlight

sentences.text: Hello everyone, welcome back to the studio, today we look at captions that actually read right.
sentences.label: filler

sentences.text: Most caption tools assume left to right text, and the moment you switch to Arabic they fall apart.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: The problem is that a line of mixed text has no single direction, and the renderer has to guess.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: When it guesses wrong, the punctuation jumps to the wrong side and the whole line looks broken.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: The fix is to stop guessing, and to mark the direction of every fragment explicitly in the output.
sentences.label: highlight

sentences.text: Each Arabic run gets an isolate, and each Latin run inside it gets one too, so the order is never ambiguous.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: That is what the caption service does now, and the difference is obvious the moment you compare them.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: You can mix an English product name into an Arabic sentence and the line still reads correctly.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: The same rule applies to the numbers, because a digit next to Arabic text is still neutral on its own.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: The second thing worth knowing is that the burned in captions are not an afterthought, they are the render.
sentences.label: highlight

sentences.text: We shape the text first, then burn it, so what you see in the preview is what ends up in the file.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: If the preview and the file ever disagreed, the whole point of the preview would be gone.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: So the pipeline measures the shaping, renders it, and then checks the result once more before it ships.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: None of this needs a cloud service, which is rather the point of doing it locally.
sentences.label: context

sentences.text: That is all for today, thanks for watching, and goodbye for now.
sentences.label: filler
